name: flow-card
description:
One step of a flow that happens away from the main product — authorising a device, confirming a purchase, recovering an account. avenID's device screen is the reference: a status glyph, an eyebrow, a heading, a description, a code to read aloud, an action, and a trust line.

It is a unit because that screen is where a user is asked to trust something, and every element on it is doing that job. The status glyph is not decoration — it is the difference between 'connected' and 'this link is broken', and on avenID it was three hand-drawn inline SVGs in a `{#if}` chain, which is three chances for the shapes to drift apart and no way for any other surface to reuse them.

base.$description: Centred and narrow. This screen has exactly one job and nothing else on it, so the measure is tight and the whole card is the focal point — the composition rule that an empty-ish screen owns its viewport rather than floating under a header.

glyph.$description: The status, as a shape. It comes from the icon registry rather than being drawn inline per branch — three hand-written SVGs in an `{#if}` chain is three chances to drift and no way for another surface to reuse them. The tinted disc is the same tint/ink pairing a badge uses, so a status here and a status in a table read as the same system.

code.$description: A code the user reads aloud or types into another device. Tabular, wide-tracked and grouped, because the failure mode here is misreading an 8 as a B — and `user-select: all` so one click selects the whole thing rather than half of it.

trust.$description: Who you are actually talking to. On a screen whose whole purpose is being trusted, this is content and not a footer — it is the sentence that answers 'should I press this'.

status.$description: Where the flow is. It dresses the GLYPH and nothing else — a whole card turning green says the page succeeded, when what succeeded is one step.

a11y.note: `aria-live="polite"` on the card, because the heading and description CHANGE as the flow advances and a screen-reader user is otherwise left on the previous step with no way to know. The alert is `role="alert"`, which interrupts — correct for a failure the user must act on. The status glyph is decorative: colour is never the only signal, so the heading always says in words what the glyph says in shape. The code is `user-select: all` so it can be copied in one gesture rather than dragged.
